record.file_problem: Repository metadata, README, and file list only; the listed paper PDF and code were not read or run.
record.tranche_reason: The README describes an audit using activation-steering and weight-space refusal repair, but does not report a test of the difference-in-means direction or the claim that a single direction mediates refusal.
record.gate_note: The README does not say that the steering vectors are the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. Reported repair and prefix results are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the claim versions. Detector AUROC and false-firing results concern the gate rather than refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The repository uses prompt-gated activation steering (built on SafeTune's CASTModel) and weight-space repair as tools to add refusal to Tiny Aya, then audits language fairness. The README never says its steering vector is the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. It induces refusal on purpose and reports only how its own threshold and gating choices perform: benign and harmful refusal by language, gate AUROC, and the effect of a greeting prefix. It does not test whether a single direction mediates refusal, its removal, transfer, or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that equal false-refusal rates across languages with differing gate-score distributions force unequal protection. Which error to equalise is a deployment decision, so they report both at matched budgets.
record.recipe_differences: The README describes a multilingual refusal-repair audit using prompt-gated activation steering, per-language or pooled split-conformal thresholds, and weight-space repair; it does not specify the original difference-in-means recipe. This is an audit-study repository.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by threshold scheme, resource tier, language, and the presence of an English greeting prefix. The README also notes that generations differ slightly across hardware and are reported separately by hardware.

fits_no_version.finding: At ε=.05, per-language conformal gate thresholds cut worst-language benign refusal from 34.9% to 25.5% versus a pooled threshold. The cost is lower harmful-prompt refusal in low-resource languages (-7.5 pp; Javanese -14.4 pp).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In gated refusal steering, equalising false-refusal across languages trades off against equal protection on harmful prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: A benign 'Good morning.' prefix raises benign refusal of steered models from about 20% to 64%, versus 11% to 13% for the unrepaired model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conditional refusal-steering gates are brittle to benign English prefixes, producing large false-refusal increases.

record.problems: This record is based on the README rather than the paper or code. The README does not provide the underlying refusal counts for several reported differences, nor uncertainty intervals for the language-specific changes or greeting-prefix comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No other refusal-rate results stated in the README were left out. Gate AUROC, false-firing bounds, keyword-detector recall, and judge-comparator results were omitted because they do not measure the refusal behavior named by the claim versions.
record.verdict_notes: Based only on the README and file list; paper/main.pdf was not available. The steering module (fitting steering vectors and condition directions) may use a difference-in-means vector. If the paper shows this, and reports multilingual refusal induction or ablation with that vector, it could bear on V1 or V6 (cross-language transfer) and should be re-read. Appendix D reports a negative cross-language CircuitKIT circuit comparison. That concerns circuits, not the refusal direction, so it is not recorded. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No stated test of the difference-in-means direction, its removal or addition, or preservation of general capabilities.
Weight-space repair is mentioned, but no result tests abliteration or removal of refusal in released models.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No test comparing a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Multilingual repair is reported, but transfer of the claimed direction across languages or model variants is not tested.
No test of how refusal-training timing or method affects existence of a removable direction.
